final_claims.pathway_name: Glycine, serine, alanine and threonine metabolism

react_result.final_narrative_text: Differential abundance analysis of nine metabolites revealed robust cross-paradigm enrichment in two interconnected pathways. The dominant signal is Glycine, serine and threonine metabolism (KEGG:hsa00260 / KEGG:map00260), which achieved the top rank in all three independent tools: RaMP-DB multi-DB ORA (FDR=1.30×10⁻⁸, fold enrichment=758, n=4 hits), MetaboAnalystR KEGG PSEA (p=0.004, n=2 hits), and Mummichog m/z-direct activity (p=0.0023, n=6 matched features). The four input driver compounds — L-threonine (KEGG:C00188), choline (KEGG:C00114), dihydrolipoate (KEGG:C02147), and L-glutamic acid (KEGG:C00025) — are all confirmed members of this pathway's metabolite roster. A second coherent signal emerges from Nicotinate and nicotinamide metabolism (KEGG:hsa00760 / KEGG:map00760), which ranks second in Mummichog (p=0.0125) and appears in both RaMP ORA (FDR=7.0×10⁻⁴) and MetaboAnalystR (p=0.046). Its driver metabolites are niacinamide (KEGG:C00153) and L-glutamic acid, the latter acting as a nitrogen-donor precursor in de novo NAD⁺ biosynthesis. L-Glutamic acid (KEGG:C00025) is the most pleiotropic driver, appearing in both pathways and providing a mechanistic bridge between amino-acid catabolism and NAD⁺ salvage. Dihydrolipoate (KEGG:C02147) anchors the energy-cofactor dimension, while choline participates in one-carbon metabolism and methyl-group transfer upstream of glycine/serine/threonine biochemistry. The convergence of a hypergeometric ORA method, a Kolmogorov–Smirnov set-enrichment method, and an empirical-compound network m/z-direct method on the same two pathways constitutes a strong consensus that treatment induces coordinated reprogramming of amino-acid carbon skeletons and nicotinamide-cofactor metabolism.

react_result.final_narrative_text: Cross-paradigm pathway analysis of nine differentially abundant metabolites identified two coherent winners. Glycine, serine and threonine metabolism (KEGG:map00260) achieved rank 0 in RaMP ORA with FDR=1.30×10⁻⁸, rank 0 in Mummichog with p=0.0051, and rank 0 in MetaboAnalystR with p=0.004. Four driver metabolites—L-threonine (KEGG:C00188), choline (KEGG:C00114), dihydrolipoate (KEGG:C02147), and L-glutamic acid (KEGG:C00025)—were present in the RaMP hit list for this pathway. The convergent evidence across ORA and m/z-direct paradigms indicates robust enrichment. Nicotinate and nicotinamide metabolism (KEGG:map00760) ranked second in RaMP ORA (FDR=6.97×10⁻⁴) and appeared in Mummichog (p=0.017) and MetaboAnalystR (p=0.046), driven by L-glutamic acid and niacinamide. RaMP ORA also detected nitrogen metabolism (KEGG:map00910, FDR=6.01×10⁻⁴) and biogenic amine synthesis (WP:WP550, FDR=5.12×10⁻⁴), both with L-glutamic acid as the sole input-metabolite hit, suggesting amino-group handling is a secondary axis of perturbation. The first pathway is the primary biological signal; the second and third are consistent secondary hits. Treatment therefore reprograms amino-acid catabolism centred on the glycine/serine/threonine hub.

  "narrative_text": "Differential abundance analysis of nine metabolites revealed robust cross-paradigm enrichment in two interconnected pathways. The dominant signal is Glycine, serine and threonine metabolism (KEGG:hsa00260 / KEGG:map00260), which achieved the top rank in all three independent tools: RaMP-DB multi-DB ORA (FDR=1.30×10⁻⁸, fold enrichment=758, n=4 hits), MetaboAnalystR KEGG PSEA (p=0.004, n=2 hits), and Mummichog m/z-direct activity (p=0.0023, n=6 matched features). The four input driver compounds — L-threonine (KEGG:C00188), choline (KEGG:C00114), dihydrolipoate (KEGG:C02147), and L-glutamic acid (KEGG:C00025) — are all confirmed members of this pathway's metabolite roster. A second coherent signal emerges from Nicotinate and nicotinamide metabolism (KEGG:hsa00760 / KEGG:map00760), which ranks second in Mummichog (p=0.0125) and appears in both RaMP ORA (FDR=7.0×10⁻⁴) and MetaboAnalystR (p=0.046). Its driver metabolites are niacinamide (KEGG:C00153) and L-glutamic acid, the latter acting as a nitrogen-donor precursor in de novo NAD⁺ biosynthesis. L-Glutamic acid (KEGG:C00025) is the most pleiotropic driver, appearing in both pathways and providing a mechanistic bridge between amino-acid catabolism and NAD⁺ salvage. final_react_result.final_narrative_text: Differential abundance analysis of nine metabolites revealed robust cross-paradigm enrichment in two interconnected pathways. The dominant signal is Glycine, serine and threonine metabolism (KEGG:hsa00260 / KEGG:map00260), which achieved the top rank in all three independent tools: RaMP-DB multi-DB ORA (FDR=1.30×10⁻⁸, fold enrichment=758, n=4 hits), MetaboAnalystR KEGG PSEA (p=0.004, n=2 hits), and Mummichog m/z-direct activity (p=0.0023, n=6 matched features). The four input driver compounds — L-threonine (KEGG:C00188), choline (KEGG:C00114), dihydrolipoate (KEGG:C02147), and L-glutamic acid (KEGG:C00025) — are all confirmed members of this pathway's metabolite roster. A second coherent signal emerges from Nicotinate and nicotinamide metabolism (KEGG:hsa00760 / KEGG:map00760), which ranks second in Mummichog (p=0.0125) and appears in both RaMP ORA (FDR=7.0×10⁻⁴) and MetaboAnalystR (p=0.046). Its driver metabolites are niacinamide (KEGG:C00153) and L-glutamic acid, the latter acting as a nitrogen-donor precursor in de novo NAD⁺ biosynthesis. L-Glutamic acid (KEGG:C00025) is the most pleiotropic driver, appearing in both pathways and providing a mechanistic bridge between amino-acid catabolism and NAD⁺ salvage. Dihydrolipoate (KEGG:C02147) anchors the energy-cofactor dimension, while choline participates in one-carbon metabolism and methyl-group transfer upstream of glycine/serine/threonine biochemistry. The convergence of a hypergeometric ORA method, a Kolmogorov–Smirnov set-enrichment method, and an empirical-compound network m/z-direct method on the same two pathways constitutes a strong consensus that treatment induces coordinated reprogramming of amino-acid carbon skeletons and nicotinamide-cofactor metabolism.
